# Failure test: Redis outage

<!-- Generated by scripts/analyze_failure_test.py. Do not edit by hand: regenerate it
     with scripts/failure-test.sh, which rewrites this file from the saved run data. -->

Generated from `docs/failure-tests/kubernetes/2026-11-10`.

## What was done

Steady load was driven against `/api/data` for the whole run. Part way through, Redis
was frozen, left frozen, and then let go. Freezing rather than stopping is the point:
connections stay open and commands simply never get an answer, which is the failure
mode the 200 ms Redis timeout and the circuit breaker exist for. Stopping the container
would have refused connections instead, which is a different failure.

On Kubernetes the freeze is SIGSTOP to the `redis-server` process, sent from the
kind node rather than from inside the pod. Kubernetes has no equivalent of
`docker compose pause`, and kind's default CNI does not enforce NetworkPolicy, so
SIGSTOP is what reproduces the failure the compose run used. It has to come from
outside the pod's PID namespace: the kernel discards an unhandled signal sent to
PID 1 from inside its own namespace, so `kubectl exec ... kill -STOP 1` does nothing
at all and Redis keeps answering.

Throughout, `/admin/circuit` was polled so the breaker's state could be timed. That
endpoint reads in-memory state and touches neither Redis nor the fallback, which is why
it keeps answering while Redis is frozen.

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Algorithm | sliding-window |
| Load users | 5 |
| Per-user limit (requests/min) | 100 |
| Offered rate | 20.0 req/s |
| Baseline before the pause | 30.0 s |
| Pause duration | 40.0 s |
| Observation after unpause | 70.0 s |
| Circuit poll interval | 100 ms |
| Breaker failure threshold | 3 consecutive Redis failures |
| Breaker open timeout | 30,000 ms |

## What was measured

A 429 is a correct answer from a rate limiter, so it is not counted as a failure here.
Failures are 5xx responses, responses with a status the service should never return,
and requests that received no response at all.

| Measure | Value |
|---------|-------|
| Requests recorded | 2,800 |
| 5xx responses | 0 |
| Requests with no response (client timeouts and connection errors) | 0 |
| Other unexpected statuses | 0 |
| Total failures | 0 (0.0%) |
| Pause to breaker observed OPEN | 687 ms |
| Unpause to breaker observed CLOSED | 20,792 ms |
| Breaker's last entry into OPEN, to observed CLOSED | 30,118 ms |

The time to close is not the time Redis took to come back. The breaker only lets a
probe through once its open timeout has elapsed, so recovery is paced by that timer
and depends on where in that cycle the recovery happens to land. The last row above
measures the breaker's own cycle instead, from the moment it last entered OPEN to
the moment it was seen CLOSED; it should sit close to the configured open timeout
of 30,000 ms. So the time between Redis becoming reachable and the
breaker closing is at worst one full open timeout, and at best immediate - it is a
property of this configuration, not a measurement of how fast Redis recovered.

Both transition times are the gap between an event this script's own log timed and
the first poll that saw the new state, so each carries up to 100 ms of
polling error and is an upper bound on the true transition time, not an exact value.

## By phase

A request belongs to the phase it was *sent* in.

| Phase | Duration | Requests | 200 | 429 | 5xx | No response | Allowed/s | Served by fallback |
|-------|----------|----------|-----|-----|-----|-------------|-----------|--------------------|
| baseline | 30.1 s | 599 | 500 | 99 | 0 | 0 | 16.6 | 0 |
| outage | 40.3 s | 806 | 802 | 4 | 0 | 0 | 19.9 | 795 |
| recovery | 69.8 s | 1,395 | 1,057 | 338 | 0 | 0 | 15.1 | 414 |

`Served by fallback` counts responses whose `X-Algorithm` header was `local-fallback`,
which is the service reporting on itself rather than an inference from the timing.

#### What the failover did to the limit

The fallback keeps its own counters and cannot read Redis's, so when the
breaker opens every caller starts a fresh window on this instance however much
of their Redis window they had already spent.

That is visible here: admissions went from 16.6 per second while
Redis was up to 19.9 per second while it was frozen, against a
configured limit that did not change. The service kept answering, which is
the point of the fallback, but it was enforcing a more generous limit than
the one it is configured with, and it says so in the `X-Algorithm` header
on every one of those responses.

### Response time by phase

Only responses that arrived are included: a request that timed out has no service
response time, and averaging the client timeout in would turn a non-answer into a slow
answer.

| Phase | Responses | p50 | p95 | p99 | max |
|-------|-----------|-----|-----|-----|-----|
| baseline | 599 | 6 ms | 9 ms | 13 ms | 30 ms |
| outage | 806 | 4 ms | 7 ms | 205 ms | 209 ms |
| recovery | 1,395 | 4 ms | 7 ms | 9 ms | 12 ms |

Times are relative to the moment Redis was paused. A negative value is before it.

| Observed state | Relative to pause |
|----------------|-------------------|
| CLOSED | -29.9 s |
| OPEN | +0.7 s |
| HALF_OPEN | +30.6 s |
| OPEN | +30.9 s |
| HALF_OPEN | +60.9 s |
| CLOSED | +61.1 s |

Polls recorded: 1,280, of which 0 got no answer.

## What this does not show

- **No availability figure.** This is a single run of about two minutes, under one
  synthetic load shape, on one machine. It cannot support a claim about availability
  over any period, and none is made here or anywhere else in this repository.
- **2 instances, and the fallback's limits are per instance.** While the
  breaker was open each replica enforced the configured limit against its own
  counters, so between them the 2 of them could admit up to 2
  times the configured rate. The admission figures above are the total across all
  of them, not one replica's.
- **The breaker is per instance too.** The state timeline above is one pod's, polled
  directly rather than through the Service, because a load-balanced poll would
  interleave independent state machines. The other replicas ran their own breakers
  over the same outage; nothing here times those.
- **One failure mode.** A frozen Redis is not the same as a Redis that refuses
  connections, returns errors, or loses data. Only the frozen case was tested.
- **The load generator shared the machine with the service**, so the response times
  above include contention that a separate generator would not cause.
